claim: Distal appendages are ninefold symmetric blade-like structures attached to the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: Distal appendages are ninefold symmetric blade-like structures attached to the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is a well-established structural description supported by the manuscript's introduction and cited literature.

claim: Distal appendages are critical for the formation of the primary cilium by regulating at least four critical steps: preciliary vesicle recruitment, recruitment and initiation of intraflagellar transport (IFT), and removal of CP110.
source: These structures are critical for the formation of the primary cilium, by regulating at least four critical steps: preciliary vesicle recruitment, recruitment and initiation of intraflagellar transport (IFT), and removal of CP110.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states these four functions in the abstract and provides experimental evidence throughout.

claim: The order of recruitment of distal appendage proteins is highly interconnected and forms a more complex hierarchy than previously described.
source: Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts, we show that the order of the recruitment of the distal appendage proteins is highly interconnected and a more complex hierarchy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments presented in Figure 2 and related data.

claim: CEP83-SCLT1 and CEP164-TTBK2 are two protein modules critical for structural assembly of distal appendages.
source: Our analysis highlights two protein modules, CEP83-SCLT1 and CEP164-TTBK2, as critical for structural assembly of distal appendages.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing these modules are essential for distal appendage organization.

claim: CEP89 selectively functions in RAB34+ vesicle recruitment.
source: Functional assays revealed that CEP89 selectively functions in the RAB34+ vesicle recruitment, while deletion of the integral components, CEP83-SCLT1-CEP164-TTBK2, severely compromised all four steps of cilium formation.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5C demonstrating CEP89's specific role in vesicle recruitment.

claim: Deletion of CEP83-SCLT1-CEP164-TTBK2 severely compromised all four steps of cilium formation.
source: Functional assays revealed that CEP89 selectively functions in the RAB34+ vesicle recruitment, while deletion of the integral components, CEP83-SCLT1-CEP164-TTBK2, severely compromised all four steps of cilium formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple functional assays in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The primary cilium is an organelle that extends from the cell surface and consists of the ninefold microtubule-based structure (or axoneme) and the ciliary membrane.
source: The primary cilium is an organelle that extends from the cell surface and consists of the ninefold microtubule-based structure (or axoneme) and the ciliary membrane (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: This is a well-established structural description of primary cilia supported by citation.

claim: The cilium serves as a sensor for extracellular environmental cues through specific membrane proteins accumulated on its membrane.
source: With specific membrane proteins (e.g. G-protein coupled receptors) accumulated on its membrane, the cilium serves as a sensor for the extracellular environmental cues (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: This functional description is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Biogenesis of the cilium is coupled to the cell cycle, with the cilium mainly forming during G0/G1 phase and disassembling prior to mitosis.
source: Biogenesis of the cilium is coupled to the cell cycle, such that the cilium mainly forms during G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle and disassembles prior to mitosis (Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982).
evidence: This is a well-established cell cycle relationship supported by citation.

claim: The cilium extends from the mother (or older) centriole during G0/G1 phase.
source: In G0/G1 phase, the cilium extends from the mother (or older) centriole, which is distinguished from the daughter (or younger) centriole by its possession of the two centriolar substructures (Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982): distal appendages and subdistal appendages (Paintrand et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on centriole biology.

claim: The mother centriole is distinguished from the daughter centriole by its possession of distal appendages and subdistal appendages.
source: In G0/G1 phase, the cilium extends from the mother (or older) centriole, which is distinguished from the daughter (or younger) centriole by its possession of the two centriolar substructures (Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982): distal appendages and subdistal appendages (Paintrand et al., 1992).
evidence: This structural distinction is supported by cited literature.

claim: Distal appendages are ninefold symmetrical blade-like structures with each blade attaching to the triplet microtubules at the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: The distal appendages are ninefold symmetrical blade-like structures with each blade attaching to the triplet microtubules at the distal end of the mother centriole (Anderson, 1972; Bowler et al., 2019; Paintrand et al., 1992).
evidence: This structural description is supported by multiple citations including electron microscopy studies.

claim: Subdistal appendages appear to be dispensable for cilium formation.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mazo et al., 2016.

claim: Distal appendages regulate ciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2012 and Sillibourne et al., 2013.

claim: Distal appendages regulate recruitment of intraflagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: Distal appendages regulate recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex, which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dateyama et al., 2019 and Kanie et al., 2017.

claim: Distal appendages regulate removal of CP110 from the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: CP110 is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension.
source: Unlike subdistal appendages, which appear to be dispensable for the cilium formation (Mazo et al., 2016), the distal appendages play crucial roles in the cilium biogenesis, through their regulation of at least four different molecular steps of the cilium formation (Graser et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013; Tanos et al., 2013): (1) ciliary vesicle recruitment (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013), (2) recruitment of intra-flagellar transport (IFT) protein complexes (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012), (3) recruitment of CEP19-RABL2 complex (Dateyama et al., 2019), which is critical for IFT initiation at the ciliary base (Kanie et al., 2017), and (4) removal of CP110 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014; Goetz et al., 2012; Tanos et al., 2013), which is believed to suppress axonemal microtubule extension (Spektor et al., 2007), from the distal end of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spektor et al., 2007.

claim: Ten proteins have been shown to localize to the distal appendages: CEP164, CEP89, CEP83, SCLT1, FBF1, TTBK2, INPP5E, LRRC45, ANKRD26, and PIDD1.
source: To date, ten proteins have been shown to localize to the distal appendages: CEP164 (Graser et al., 2007), CEP89 (also known as CCDC123) (Sillibourne et al., 2013; Sillibourne et al., 2011), CEP83 (Tanos et al., 2013), SCLT1 (Tanos et al., 2013), FBF1 (Tanos et al., 2013), TTBK2 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014), INPP5E (Xu et al., 2016), LRRC45 (Kurtulmus et al., 2018), ANKRD26 (Bowler et al., 2019), and PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a compilation of previously published findings, each supported by specific citations.

claim: CEP83 sits at the top of the distal appendage protein hierarchy and recruits SCLT1 and CEP89.
source: These proteins are recruited to the distal appendages in hierarchical order, where CEP83 sits at the top of the hierarchy and recruits SCLT1 and CEP89 (Tanos et al., 2013).
evidence: This hierarchical relationship is supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: SCLT1 recruits CEP164, ANKRD26, and LRRC45.
source: SCLT1 recruits CEP164 (Tanos et al., 2013), ANKRD26 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021), and LRRC45 (Kurtulmus et al., 2018).
evidence: This hierarchical relationship is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CEP164 recruits TTBK2.
source: CEP164 recruits TTBK2 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014).
evidence: This hierarchical relationship is supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claim: Three new distal appendage proteins were identified: KIZ, NCS1, and CEP15.
source: Here, we identify three more distal appendage proteins (KIZ, NCS1, and CEP15).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript.

claim: CEP15 was previously named C3ORF14.
source: CEP15 was previously named as C3ORF14, and we renamed it to CEP15 to reflect its function.
evidence: This is a nomenclature clarification provided by the authors.

claim: Two independent studies determined the precise localization of classical distal appendage proteins using STORM.
source: Recently, two independent studies determined the precise localization of the classical distal appendage proteins (CEP164, CEP83, SCLT1, FBF1, CEP89, TTBK2, and ANKRD26) using Stochastic Optical Reconstruction Microscopy (STORM) (Bowler et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowler et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: 3D-SIM has inferior lateral (xy) resolution compared to STORM but offers flexibility in fluorophore selection and sample preparation for multi-color imaging.
source: While the lateral (xy) resolution of 3D-SIM is inferior to that of STORM, the flexibility of fluorophore selection and sample preparation for multi-color imaging by 3D-SIM (Valli et al., 2021) allows us to easily locate target proteins relative to multiple centriolar markers.
evidence: This is a technical comparison supported by citation to Valli et al., 2021.

claim: FBF1 localizes between adjacent CEP164 structures in the axial view, identifying it as a distal appendage matrix protein.
source: As an example, the localization of FBF1, which was positioned between adjacent CEP164 structures seen in the axial view of the published STORM picture (which the authors thus identified FBF1 as a distal appendage matrix protein) (Yang et al., 2018), was also recapitulated in our SIM image (see FBF1 top view in Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by both citation to Yang et al., 2018 and the authors' own SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CEP89 localizes near the subdistal appendage in addition to its distal appendage localization.
source: We also observed localization of CEP89 near the subdistal appendage in addition to its distal appendage localization (CEP89 side view in Figure 1A), consistent with the previous report (Chong et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' imaging data in Figure 1A and citations to Chong et al., 2020 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: CEP83 was shown to localize to the innermost position of the distal appendage when detected with an antibody recognizing the C-terminal region.
source: CEP83 was shown to localize to the innermost position of the distal appendage (Bowler et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018). We recapitulated this localization (see CEP83 inner ring in Figure 1A; Figure 1B) with the antibody used in the previous two papers (Bowler et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018), which recognizes the C-terminal region of CEP83 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowler et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2018, and the authors' own data in Figure 1A.

claim: The peak-to-peak diameter of the inner CEP83 ring is 308.6±4.9 nm.
source: The peak-to-peak diameter of the inner CEP83 ring (308.6±4.9 nm, Figure 1C) was comparable to the previous report (313±20 nm) (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' data shown in Figure 1C, compared to a cited value.

claim: When detected with an antibody recognizing the middle part of CEP83, the protein localizes to a ring at the outermost part of the distal appendage with a diameter of 513.4±9.0 nm.
source: However, when we detected this protein with the antibody that detects the middle part of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), we observed the ring located at the outermost part of the distal appendage with the diameter of 513.4±9.0 nm (see CEP83 outer ring in Figure 1A; Figure 1B; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and 1C.

claim: Both CEP83 antibodies recognized a specific band at 80-110 kDa that is lost in CEP83 knockout cells.
source: Both antibodies recognized the specific band at 80–110 kDa that is lost in the CEP83 knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CEP83 may have an extended configuration that spans 100 nm in length.
source: One intriguing explanation for the difference in the ring diameter is that the protein might have an extended configuration that spans 100 nm (the difference in radius between inner and outer ring) in length.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the diameter measurements and structural predictions.

claim: Human CEP83 protein is predicted to contain two conserved coiled-coil domains, one of which may span between 40-633 amino acids.
source: Human CEP83 protein (Q9Y592) is predicted to contain two conserved coiled-coil domains, one of which may span between 40–633 amino acids.
evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction.

claim: The AlphaFold model of CEP83 shows a highly extended alpha-helical structure conserved among most species.
source: Examination of the AlphaFold model (Jumper et al., 2021) of CEP83 shows a consistent highly extended alpha-helical structure, conserved among most species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting the model of CEP83 as a highly extended molecule.
evidence: This is supported by AlphaFold structural predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and cited by Jumper et al., 2021.

claim: One alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid.
source: Since one alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid (Pauling et al., 1951) and contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm (Ainavarapu et al., 2007), 400 amino acids stretch of coiled-coil domain as well as a disordered region that consists of 40 amino acids (the maximum distance between antigens of the two CEP83 antibodies) could contribute at least 76 nm.
evidence: This is based on established structural parameters of alpha helices cited from Pauling et al., 1951 and Ainavarapu et al., 2007.

claim: The contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm.
source: Since one alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid (Pauling et al., 1951) and contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm (Ainavarapu et al., 2007), 400 amino acids stretch of coiled-coil domain as well as a disordered region that consists of 40 amino acids (the maximum distance between antigens of the two CEP83 antibodies) could contribute at least 76 nm.
evidence: This is based on established structural parameters cited from Ainavarapu et al., 2007.

claim: The length of immunoglobulin G (IgG) is approximately 8 nm.
source: Since the length of immunoglobulin G (IgG) is ~8 nm (see Figure 2 of Tan et al., 2008), the primary and secondary antibodies at the two edges could contribute another ~30 nm.
evidence: This is based on established antibody dimensions cited from Tan et al., 2008.

claim: CEP83 forms an extended backbone scaffolding the distal appendage.
source: This model, wherein CEP83 forms an extended backbone scaffolding the distal appendage, is attractive given that CEP83 is important for localization of all the other distal appendage proteins (Tanos et al., 2013) to different positions along the distal appendages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data and supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: GFP fused to the C-terminus of CEP83 (CEP83-GFP) localized to a more inward and more basal centriolar position than CEP164 with a peak-to-peak diameter of 339.7±18.4 nm.
source: Consistent with the endogenous CEP83 detected with the antibody that recognizes C-terminus of the protein, GFP fused to the C-terminus of CEP83 (CEP83-GFP) localized to more inward and more basal centriolar position than CEP164 with the peak-to-peak diameter of 339.7±18.4 nm, when the GFP was detected by antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: GFP attached to the N-terminus of CEP83 (GFP-CEP83) was located at a similar position to CEP164 with a diameter of 425.5±17.5 nm.
source: GFP attached to the N-terminus of CEP83 (GFP-CEP83) was located at the similar position to CEP164 with the diameter of 425.5±17.5 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-D.

claim: PIDD1 localizes to a ring with a similar diameter to CEP164 but is displaced distally in the side view.
source: For the recently identified distal appendage protein, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021), we observe a ring with a similar diameter to CEP164 but that was displaced distally in the side view (see PIDD1 in Figure 1A; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A and 1B, and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claim: PIDD1 localization is consistent with the localization of its functional partner ANKRD26.
source: This localization is consistent with the localization of its functional partner ANKRD26 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 1A; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A and 1B, and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claim: KIZ localizes to a similar position as ANKRD26-PIDD1.
source: KIZ (or Kizuna) was localized to the similar position to ANKRD26-PIDD1.
evidence: This is based on the authors' localization studies.

claim: LRRC45 is located at the innermost region of the distal appendage with the smallest ring diameter.
source: LRRC45 was located at the innermost region of the distal appendage with the smallest ring diameter (Figure 1A; Figure 1B; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A, 1B, and 1C.

claim: LRRC45 localization is similar to that of the inner ring of CEP83.
source: This localization is similar to that of the inner ring of CEP83.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the authors' localization data.

claim: INPP5E was reported to localize to the distal appendage in cells grown with serum and redistribute to the cilium upon serum starvation.
source: INPP5E was reported to localize to the distal appendage in the cells grown with serum and redistribute to the cilium once cells form the organelle upon serum starvation (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: INPP5E physically interacts with CEP164.
source: This localization is also supported by the physical interaction between INPP5E and the distal appendage protein, CEP164 (Humbert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Humbert et al., 2012.

claim: INPP5E signal was observed around CEP164 in cells grown with serum, but a ninefold ring was rarely observed.
source: Indeed, we observed the INPP5E signal around the distal appendage protein CEP164 in cells grown with serum, however, we rarely observed a ninefold ring (INPP5E in Figure 1A), typically observed with all other distal appendage proteins.
evidence: This is based on the authors' imaging observations in Figure 1A.

claim: INPP5E is not a stable component of distal appendages and instead transiently localizes around the distal appendage.
source: Therefore, we were unable to measure the diameter of the ring formed by INPP5E. From this result, we think INPP5E is at least not a stable component of distal appendages and instead transiently localizes around the distal appendage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' imaging observations.

claim: Localization of one set of distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) was significantly enhanced following serum starvation.
source: Localization of one set of the distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) were significantly enhanced following the serum starvation, whereas another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) were not affected (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: Localization of another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) was not affected by serum starvation.
source: Localization of one set of the distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) were significantly enhanced following the serum starvation, whereas another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) were not affected (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: SCLT1 was the only distal appendage protein that decreased its centrosomal signal upon serum deprivation.
source: SCLT1 was the only protein that decreased its centrosomal signal upon serum deprivation.
evidence: This is based on the authors' quantitative analysis.

claim: The centrosomal signal of all distal appendage proteins was barely or not detected in their respective knockout cells.
source: In most cases, the centrosomal signal of distal appendage proteins were barely or not detected in their respective knockout cells (see for example Figure 2A, G, I), confirming that the antibodies detect specific proteins and that the semi-automated intensity measurement was working properly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantification data in Figure 2.

claim: A weak signal of FBF1 was detected in FBF1 knockout cells despite the signal looking specific.
source: Centriolar FBF1 signal looked specific as it is almost completely lost in CEP83 knockout cells, however, a weak signal of FBF1 was detected in FBF1 knockout cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: Both FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) in both alleles.
source: Since both two FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion in both alleles between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) (Table 1B), which results in a premature stop codon at the codon 61, we assumed that the knockout cells express truncated protein via either alternative translation or alternative splicing.
evidence: This is based on genomic DNA sequencing data presented in Table 1B.

claim: The FBF1 knockout mutation results in a premature stop codon at codon 61.
source: Since both two FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion in both alleles between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) (Table 1B), which results in a premature stop codon at the codon 61, we assumed that the knockout cells express truncated protein via either alternative translation or alternative splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic sequence data.

claim: CEP83 is the most upstream distal appendage protein.
source: Consistent with the original study mapping new distal appendage proteins (Tanos et al., 2013), the centrosomal signal intensity of all the knockout cells were greatly diminished in CEP83 knockout cells (Figure 2A–K; Figure 2M), confirming that CEP83 is the most upstream.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2 and supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: SCLT1 depletion showed substantial loss of localization of all other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89.
source: SCLT1 depletion also showed substantial loss of localization of all the other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89 (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2F), suggesting that CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2.

claim: CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
source: SCLT1 depletion also showed substantial loss of localization of all the other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89 (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2F), suggesting that CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the knockout data in Figure 2.

claim: SCLT1 knockout affected the localization of the outer ring of CEP83 much more strongly than the inner ring population.
source: Note that the SCLT1 knockout affected the localization of the outer ring of CEP83 much more strongly than the inner ring population (Figure 2B; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The effect of SCLT1 knockouts was much stronger than previously reported using siRNA, likely because of complete absence of the protein in the knockout system.
source: We observed a much stronger effect of SCLT1 knockouts than the previous report (Tanos et al., 2013), which used siRNA to deplete SCLT1, likely because of the complete absence of the protein in our knockout system.
evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' data and a cited study, with an interpretation of the difference.

claim: TTBK2 localization at the distal appendage is largely dependent on CEP164.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014), TTBK2 localization at the distal appendage was largely dependent on CEP164, as the TTBK2 signal in CEP164 knockout cells was at an undetectable level similar to TTBK2 knockout cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2H and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claim: TTBK2 knockout affected localization of CEP164, the outer ring CEP83, FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1.
source: Downstream of CEP164, TTBK2 knockout affected localization of CEP164, the outer ring CEP83, FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 (Figure 2A; Figure 2C; Figure 2E; Figure 2G; Figure 2K; Figure 2M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The decrease of CEP164 intensity in TTBK2 knockout cells is consistent with CEP164 being a substrate of TTBK2.
source: The decrease of CEP164 intensity in TTBK2 knockout cells is consistent with the observation that CEP164 is a substrate of TTBK2 and that centriolar CEP164 localization was markedly increased upon overexpression of wild type but not kinase-dead TTBK2 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' data and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claim: CEP83 is a substrate of TTBK2.
source: Interestingly, localization of another TTBK2 substrate, CEP83 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), was also affected by TTBK2 depletion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernatik et al., 2020 and Lo et al., 2019, and demonstrated by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout.
source: Since only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout, we predict that CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 induces a conformational change of CEP83 enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knockout data and is used to support a prediction.

claim: CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 may induce a conformational change enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
source: Since only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout, we predict that CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 induces a conformational change of CEP83 enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' data.

claim: FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 may be potential substrates of TTBK2, or their localization may be affected by phosphorylation of CEP83 or CEP164.
source: The localization changes of FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 also suggest that these proteins may be potential substrates of TTBK2, or the localization of these proteins may be affected by phosphorylation of CEP83 or CEP164.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the authors' observations of localization changes.

claim: The effect of TTBK2 depletion emphasizes that CEP164-TTBK2 complex organizes a positive feedback loop for other distal appendage proteins to maintain structural integrity.
source: In any case, the effect of TTBK2 depletion emphasizes that CEP164-TTBK2 complex (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014) organizes a positive feedback loop for other distal appendage proteins to maintain the structural integrity of the distal appendages (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' data and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claim: ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected its functional partner PIDD1.
source: Interestingly, ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected not only its functional partner, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 2K), but also the outer ring of CEP83 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2K and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claim: ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected the outer ring of CEP83.
source: Interestingly, ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected not only its functional partner, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 2K), but also the outer ring of CEP83 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: ANKRD26 may be crucial for maintaining the protein structure of CEP83 at the outer part of the distal appendages.
source: This might suggest that ANKRD26 may be crucial for maintaining the protein structure of CEP83 at the outer part of the distal appendages.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the knockout data.

claim: The diminished CEP164 level in ANKRD26 knockout cells might be explained by its direct effect or an indirect effect through the outer ring of CEP83.
source: The diminished CEP164 level in ANKRD26 knockout cells (Figure 2A; Figure 2M) might be explained by its direct effect or an indirect effect through the outer ring of CEP83.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the knockout data in Figure 2A and 2M.

claim: LRRC45 knockout did not affect FBF1 localization, contrary to a previous publication.
source: In contrast to a previous publication (Kurtulmus et al., 2018), we did not see the effect of LRRC45 on FBF1 localization (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on the authors' knockout data in Figure 2E and contrasts with a cited study.

claim: The difference between the current study and Kurtulmus et al., 2018 regarding LRRC45's effect on FBF1 might come from differences in experimental setting (siRNA versus knockout).
source: This difference might come from the difference in the experimental setting (e.g. siRNA versus knockout).
evidence: This is a speculation about the source of discrepancy between studies.

claim: The signal intensity of subdistal appendage marker CEP170 was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins.
source: The signal intensity of a marker of the subdistal appendage, CEP170, was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins (Figure 2L) suggesting that distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins at least in terms of signal intensity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 2L.

claim: Distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins in terms of signal intensity.
source: The signal intensity of a marker of the subdistal appendage, CEP170, was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins (Figure 2L) suggesting that distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins at least in terms of signal intensity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data in Figure 2L.

claim: The localization changes of distal appendage proteins were mostly not due to changes in expression level except that KIZ was highly destabilized in SCLT1 knockout cells.
source: The localization changes were mostly not due to the changes in the expression level except that protein KIZ was highly destabilized in SCLT1 knockout cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Depletion of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, or TTBK2 severely disrupted cilium formation in 24- or 48-hour serum-starved cells.
source: The depletion of each component that is important for structural integrity of distal appendages (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, TTBK2) severely disrupted the cilium formation in either 24- or 48 hr serum-starved cells (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hours after serum removal.
source: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hr after serum removal (Figure 5A), but the ciliation defect in the knockout cells were ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hr) following serum starvation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The ciliation defect in FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 knockout cells was ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hours) following serum starvation.
source: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hr after serum removal (Figure 5A), but the ciliation defect in the knockout cells were ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hr) following serum starvation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 are important for cilium formation, but cells can compensate for their lack and slowly form primary cilia.
source: This suggests that these proteins are important for cilium formation, but that cells can compensate for the lack of these proteins and slowly catch up to form primary cilia.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ciliation assay data.

claim: KIZ, LRRC45, and INPP5E had no effect on cilium formation.
source: The distal appendage protein KIZ and LRRC45, as well as the distal appendage-associated protein, INPP5E, had no effect on cilium formation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Ciliary length was mildly affected in FBF1 and INPP5E knockout cells at 24 hours.
source: Ciliary length was mildly affected in FBF1 and INPP5E knockout cells at the earlier time point (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliary length measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Shorter ciliary length was observed in ANKRD26 knockout cells serum starved for either 24 or 48 hours.
source: Shorter ciliary length was observed in ANKRD26 knockout cells serum starved for either 24 or 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliary length measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ARL13B signal intensity inside the cilium was diminished in FBF1, CEP89, or ANKRD26 knockout cells even after 48 hours of serum starvation.
source: Interestingly, ARL13B signal intensity inside the cilium was diminished in FBF1, CEP89, or ANKRD26 knockout cells even after the cells largely caught up on cilium formation after 48 hr of serum starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ARL13B intensity measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 knockouts can slowly form cilia, but the slowly formed cilia may not be functionally normal.
source: This suggests that these knockouts can slowly form cilia, but the slowly formed cilia may not be functionally normal.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ARL13B intensity data.

claim: The stronger defect in ciliary ARL13B signal in ANKRD26 might suggest a direct role of this protein in ARL13B recruitment around the distal appendages.
source: The stronger defect in ciliary ARL13B signal in ANKRD26 might suggest a direct role of this protein in ARL13B recruitment around the distal appendages.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the ARL13B intensity data.

claim: CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 severely disrupted preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: Consistent with their critical role in the structural integrity of the distal appendages, CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 severely disrupted preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: CEP89 modestly but significantly affected preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: Interestingly, CEP89 but not the other distal appendage proteins modestly but significantly affected preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: The importance of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment is largely consistent with a previous report.
source: The importance of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment is largely consistent with a previous report (Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with a cited study.

claim: CP110 removal was severely affected in knockouts of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2.
source: CP110 removal was again severely affected in knockouts of the four integral components of the distal appendages (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CP110 removal assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: CEP89 depletion partially inhibited CP110 removal.
source: CEP89 depletion partially inhibited CP110 removal (Figure 5D), correlating with the partial effect on preciliary vesicle recruitment, which is upstream of CP110 removal (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CP110 removal assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: IFT88 recruitment was severely disturbed in knockouts of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2, but not in other knockouts.
source: IFT88 recruitment was severely disturbed in the knockouts of the four integral components (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2), but not in the other knockouts (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IFT88 recruitment data in Figure 5E.

claim: The effect of CEP164 or TTBK2 on IFT88 recruitment was slightly stronger than CEP83 or SCLT1.
source: The effect of CEP164 or TTBK2 was slightly stronger than CEP83 or SCLT1, suggesting that CEP164 and TTBK2 may be more directly involved in this process.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the IFT88 recruitment data.

claim: CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2.
source: CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2 (Figure 5F), but was only mildly affected by CEP83-SCLT1, which recruit CEP164 to the distal appendages (Figure 2A and N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CEP19 recruitment data in Figure 5F.

claim: CEP19 recruitment was only mildly affected by CEP83-SCLT1.
source: CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2 (Figure 5F), but was only mildly affected by CEP83-SCLT1, which recruit CEP164 to the distal appendages (Figure 2A and N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CEP19 recruitment data in Figure 5F.

claim: A very small amount of centriolar CEP164-TTBK2 may be sufficient to bring CEP19 near the distal appendage.
source: This indicates that a very small amount of centriolar CEP164-TTBK2 may be sufficient to bring CEP19 near the distal appendage, and that CEP164-TTBK2, rather than CEP83-SCLT1, more directly regulates CEP19 recruitment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the CEP19 recruitment data.

claim: CEP164-TTBK2, rather than CEP83-SCLT1, more directly regulates CEP19 recruitment.
source: This indicates that a very small amount of centriolar CEP164-TTBK2 may be sufficient to bring CEP19 near the distal appendage, and that CEP164-TTBK2, rather than CEP83-SCLT1, more directly regulates CEP19 recruitment.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the CEP19 recruitment data.

claim: The CEP83-SCLT1 structural module brings CEP164-TTBK2 to stabilize the distal appendages.
source: In summary, the CEP83-SCLT1 structural module brings CEP164-TTBK2 to stabilize the distal appendages, and the CEP164-TTBK2 complex plays a more direct role in the cilium formation by regulating downstream processes including preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT; CEP19 recruitment, and CP110 removal.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the functional assay data.

claim: The CEP164-TTBK2 complex plays a more direct role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT and CEP19 recruitment, and CP110 removal.
source: In summary, the CEP83-SCLT1 structural module brings CEP164-TTBK2 to stabilize the distal appendages, and the CEP164-TTBK2 complex plays a more direct role in the cilium formation by regulating downstream processes including preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT; CEP19 recruitment, and CP110 removal.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the functional assay data.

claim: CEP89 is dispensable for structural integrity of the distal appendages but plays a crucial role in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: In contrast, CEP89 is dispensable for structural integrity of the distal appendages, but it instead plays a crucial role in the preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the functional assay data and presented in Figure 6.

claim: RAB34 localizes to the centriole-associated vesicle.
source: A recent paper suggested that the small GTPase RAB34, localizes to the centriole-associated vesicle (Stuck et al., 2021) and is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment/formation (Xu et al., 2018) or for fusion of the distal appendage vesicle (Ganga et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stuck et al., 2021, Xu et al., 2018, and Ganga et al., 2021.

claim: RAB34 is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment/formation.
source: A recent paper suggested that the small GTPase RAB34, localizes to the centriole-associated vesicle (Stuck et al., 2021) and is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment/formation (Xu et al., 2018) or for fusion of the distal appendage vesicle (Ganga et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: RAB34 is important for fusion of the distal appendage vesicle.
source: A recent paper suggested that the small GTPase RAB34, localizes to the centriole-associated vesicle (Stuck et al., 2021) and is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment/formation (Xu et al., 2018) or for fusion of the distal appendage vesicle (Ganga et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ganga et al., 2021.

claim: Most RAB34-positive centrioles have MYO5A at the centriole and vice versa.
source: We found that MYO5A and RAB34 localization are highly coupled. Most RAB34-positive centrioles have MYO5A at the centriole and vice versa (Figure 3A; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The percentage of RAB34 and MYO5A double positive centrioles was highest in confluent cells grown with serum and decreased upon serum starvation.
source: Note that the percentage of RAB34 and MYO5A double positive centrioles was highest in the confluent cells grown with serum and was decreased upon serum starvation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 3B.

claim: There was no difference in the percentage of RAB34 positive centrioles between subconfluent and confluent cells.
source: We did not see the difference in the percentage of RAB34 positive centrioles between cells grown to 40–50% confluency (subconfluent) and 100% confluency (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), confirming that the presence of RAB34 positive centrioles is not due to the confluency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The presence of the ciliary vesicle at the centriole before induction of cilium formation is consistent with a previous electron microscopy study.
source: The presence of the ciliary vesicle at the centriole before induction of cilium formation is consistent with the previous electron microscopy study (Figure 5D of Insinna et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Insinna et al., 2019.

claim: EHD1 and PACSIN2 were recruited to the centrosome at later time points after serum withdrawal.
source: Vesicular fusion regulators, EHD1 and PACSIN2, were recruited to the centrosome at later time points after serum withdrawal (Figure 3C; Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–H), confirming that both MYO5A and RAB34 are the earliest markers of the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) to date.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-H.

claim: Both MYO5A and RAB34 are the earliest markers of the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) to date.
source: Vesicular fusion regulators, EHD1 and PACSIN2, were recruited to the centrosome at later time points after serum withdrawal (Figure 3C; Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–H), confirming that both MYO5A and RAB34 are the earliest markers of the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) to date.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal recruitment data.

claim: RAB34 did not localize to the pericentriolar region, in contrast to MYO5A.
source: Importantly, and in contrast to MYO5A, RAB34 did not localize to the pericentriolar region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RAB34 is a more suitable vesicle marker than MYO5A to assess preciliary vesicle recruitment at the distal appendages.
source: This makes RAB34 a more suitable vesicle marker to assess preciliary vesicle recruitment at the distal appendages.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the localization specificity of RAB34.

claim: Rab34-/- mice exhibit polydactyly and cleft palate as well as perinatal lethality, phenotypes reminiscent of cilia defects.
source: Consistent with this, Rab34-/- mice exhibit polydactyly and cleft palate as well as perinatal lethality, phenotypes reminiscent of cilia defects (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: RAB34 localization was distal to CEP164 and was displaced inwardly.
source: In the 3D-SIM images, RAB34 localization was distal to CEP164 (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and was displaced inwardly (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D-SIM imaging data in Figure 3E, 3F, and supplementary figures.

claim: RAB34 localization is reminiscent of the relative positioning between the vesicle and the distal appendages seen in electron microscopy.
source: This is reminiscent of the relative positioning between the vesicle and the distal appendages seen in electron microscopy (Insinna et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited electron microscopy studies.

claim: The shape of RAB34 positive vesicles was highly variable even before cilium formation was induced by serum starvation.
source: The shape of RAB34 positive vesicles were highly variable even before the cilium formation was induced by serum starvation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G-J.

claim: MYO5A distribution was located at the edge of the RAB34 distribution on the vesicle.
source: This data showed that the MYO5A distribution was located at the edge of the RAB34 distribution on the vesicle (Figure 3H–K), with a 3D separation between the center of masses of the distributions of 89 nm and 67 nm in samples 1 and 2, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging data in Figure 3H-K and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 3D separation between the center of masses of MYO5A and RAB34 distributions was 89 nm and 67 nm in samples 1 and 2, respectively.
source: This data showed that the MYO5A distribution was located at the edge of the RAB34 distribution on the vesicle (Figure 3H–K), with a 3D separation between the center of masses of the distributions of 89 nm and 67 nm in samples 1 and 2, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a measurement from super-resolution imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The sizes of the RAB34 distributions were 230 nm x 170 nm x 190 nm for sample 1 and 190 nm × 170 nm × 250 nm for sample 2.
source: The sizes of the RAB34 distributions, reflecting the measure of vesicle sizes, were found to be 230 nm x 170 nm x 190 nm for sample 1 and 190 nm × 170 nm × 250 nm for sample 2 reported as the 1/e2 of Gaussian fits of these distributions.
evidence: This is a measurement from super-resolution imaging data.

claim: RAB34 is a more specific marker for the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) than MYO5A.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that RAB34 is a more specific marker for the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) than MYO5A and is located at a distinct position from MYO5A on the vesicle.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the localization and super-resolution data.

claim: RAB34 is located at a distinct position from MYO5A on the vesicle.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that RAB34 is a more specific marker for the centriole-associated vesicle (likely the distal appendage vesicle) than MYO5A and is located at a distinct position from MYO5A on the vesicle.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the super-resolution data.

claim: Distal appendages can minimally regulate four steps required for cilium formation: preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT recruitment to the basal body, IFT initiation by recruiting CEP19-RABL2, and CP110 removal.
source: Distal appendages can minimally regulate four steps required for cilium formation: preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT recruitment to the basal body, IFT initiation by recruiting CEP19-RABL2, and CP110 removal.
evidence: This is a summary of established functions of distal appendages.

claim: Depletion of RAB34 significantly inhibited the formation of the cilium.
source: In contrast to MYO5A depletion, which did not affect ciliogenesis, depletion of RAB34 significantly inhibited the formation of the cilium (Figure 4A), as described (Ganga et al., 2021; Oguchi et al., 2020; Stuck et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 4A and supported by multiple citations.

claim: MYO5A depletion did not affect ciliogenesis.
source: In contrast to MYO5A depletion, which did not affect ciliogenesis, depletion of RAB34 significantly inhibited the formation of the cilium (Figure 4A), as described (Ganga et al., 2021; Oguchi et al., 2020; Stuck et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: The absence of ciliation defects in MYO5A knockout cells differs from a previous observation but is consistent with the fact that mutations in MYO5A gene cause Griscelli syndrome, which has phenotypes distinct from ciliopathies.
source: The absence of ciliation defects in MYO5A knockout cells differs from the previous observation (Wu et al., 2018), but is consistent with the fact that mutations in MYO5A gene cause Griscelli syndrome (Pastural et al., 1997), of which phenotypes are distinct from ciliopathies.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the authors' data with cited literature.

claim: Only one out of 18 mother centrioles in RAB34-depleted cells had a vesicle after 3 hours of serum starvation, while 16 out of 41 control cells had vesicle(s) attached to centrioles.
source: Electron microscopy analysis of RPE cells serum-starved for 3 hr revealed that only one out of 18 mother centrioles in RAB34-depleted cells had a vesicle, while 16 out of 41 control (sgGFP) cells had the vesicle(s) attached to centrioles (p<0.0054 in Fisher's exact test) (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: RAB34 is important for initial recruitment/formation of the vesicle.
source: This suggests that RAB34 is important for initial recruitment/formation of the vesicle, in agreement with the previous report (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the electron microscopy data and supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: Removal of CP110 from the mother centriole was modestly affected in RAB34 knockout cells.
source: Removal of CP110 from the mother centriole was modestly affected in RAB34 knockout cells (Figure 4D), whereas IFT and CEP19 recruitment was not affected (Figure 4E–F), suggesting that preciliary vesicle recruitment is partially important to trigger CP110 removal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CP110 removal assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: IFT and CEP19 recruitment was not affected in RAB34 knockout cells.
source: Removal of CP110 from the mother centriole was modestly affected in RAB34 knockout cells (Figure 4D), whereas IFT and CEP19 recruitment was not affected (Figure 4E–F), suggesting that preciliary vesicle recruitment is partially important to trigger CP110 removal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IFT and CEP19 recruitment data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Preciliary vesicle recruitment is partially important to trigger CP110 removal.
source: Removal of CP110 from the mother centriole was modestly affected in RAB34 knockout cells (Figure 4D), whereas IFT and CEP19 recruitment was not affected (Figure 4E–F), suggesting that preciliary vesicle recruitment is partially important to trigger CP110 removal.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the functional assay data.

claim: IFT52 depletion greatly diminished the localization of all other IFT complex proteins tested and inhibited cilium formation.
source: As expected, IFT52 depletion greatly diminished the localization of all the other IFT complex proteins tested and thus inhibited the cilium formation (Figure 4G–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IFT protein localization and ciliation assay data in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: FOP depletion abrogated the localization of CEP19 and IFT88 as well as cilium formation.
source: Similarly, FOP depletion abrogated the localization of CEP19 and IFT88 as well as cilium formation (Figure 4I,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CEP19 and IFT88 localization and ciliation assay data in Figure 4I, J, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Depletion of neither FOP nor IFT52 disrupted preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: Depletion of neither FOP nor IFT52 disrupted the preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 4K), suggesting that preciliary vesicle recruitment can proceed independently of the IFT-CEP19 pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data in Figure 4K.

claim: Preciliary vesicle recruitment can proceed independently of the IFT-CEP19 pathway.
source: Depletion of neither FOP nor IFT52 disrupted the preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 4K), suggesting that preciliary vesicle recruitment can proceed independently of the IFT-CEP19 pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data.

claim: Distal appendages independently regulate preciliary vesicle and IFT/CEP19 recruitment, whereas CP110 removal is partially downstream of preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: In summary, our data suggest that distal appendages independently regulate preciliary vesicle and IFT; CEP19 recruitment, whereas CP110 removal is partially downstream of preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the functional assay data and presented in Figure 4L.
